comparison: Use the period-one additive circle for rotations and its normalized Haar law, retaining f_g(t)=f(t+g). The complex Fourier Hilbert basis provides infrastructure but must be converted to the source real constant, sqrt(2) cosine and sqrt(2) sine basis. Restrict to L>=1 and retain dimension 2L+1, the constant block and the displayed harmonic blocks [[cos,sin],[-sin,cos]], whose signs follow from the positive shift convention. BlockDiagonal' constructs the representation after reindexing its mixed one- and two-dimensional blocks. Gaussian coefficient noise uses variance sigma squared, not sigma as variance, and is independent across coefficients and of the sampled rotation in the stated experiment. The Gaussian-process mean/covariance display depending on g describes the conditional-on-rotation white-noise experiment; marginalizing a random rotation generally gives a Gaussian mixture, not a Gaussian process with that same deterministic mean/covariance. The infinite white-noise representation, real-basis equivalence and finite sufficient observation reduction require proofs; no specialized multireference-alignment theorem was located in the inspected sources. Preserve the original missing-dt display as a recorded source convention.

comparison: Define the comparison by all convex scalar test functions on R^d for the admitted finite-first-moment measures, including its later use on subprobabilities. ConvexOn supplies the test predicate but ordinary setwise Measure order is not this relation. Both signs of affine tests imply equal total mass and first moments where the tests are integrable; hence subprobabilities of unequal mass cannot be compared by this definition. Finite first moments do not make every convex test integrable. A proper extended-integral convention can retain positive infinity after subtracting an integrable affine lower bound; a totalized real Bochner integral returning zero outside integrability would give a different order. Do not restrict the tests to nonnegative or bounded convex functions without an equivalence proof. The random-variable notation compares their laws and does not require a specified coupling or pointwise order. No dedicated convex-order declaration was found in the searched Probability/Convex sources.
gap: Convexity and integration are available, but the convex-order predicate needs an explicit extended-integral test convention and its measure-law identifications.

comparison: Form gamma as the joint pushforward under Q of the L Radon-Nikodym density coordinates, retaining the admitted domination/integrability conditions needed for real finite representatives and their mean-one property. The feasible set consists of probability measures on R^L concentrated on the NONNEGATIVE diagonal {t*1_L:t>=0}, including the origin, and below gamma in the source convex order. It is not the full positive orthant or the earlier one-dimensional set of all real laws. Support containment in this closed diagonal can be related to measure concentration under the ambient Euclidean Borel setting; it should not be confused with merely mean-on-diagonal. Set.ofPred and ProbabilityMeasure supply the set wrapper, while the convex-order comparison retains its extended-integral convention from D5. The displayed maximum in a partial order is an optimization goal, not by itself a proof of a greatest element, existence or uniqueness, and must not be reduced to maximizing a selected scalar moment.
gap: Probability measures, pushforward and support restrictions express the feasible-set construction, with convex-order conventions and existence of an order maximum still to establish.
